title: Tokens per second and entropy-coded bitrate
goal:
Compute how many tokens per second EnCodec produces and what an entropy coder can save (Sections 3.1, 3.2, and 3.3).

- `tokens_per_second(fs, strides, n_q)` returns tokens per second: latent steps per second, `fs / prod(strides)`, times `n_q`.
- `bitrate_kbps(fs, strides, n_q, n_codes=1024)` returns the fixed-length bitrate in kbps.
- `n_q_for_kbps(kbps, fs, strides, n_codes=1024)` returns the number of codebooks that gives exactly that bandwidth, and raises `ValueError` if no whole number of codebooks does.
- `entropy_kbps(probs, fs, strides)` takes `probs`, an `(n_q, n_codes)` array in which row `q` is the probability distribution of codebook `q`. The language model of Section 3.3 predicts each codebook separately and ignores the dependence between codebooks at one step, so the ideal entropy-coded bitrate is the sum over codebooks of the entropy in bits, times the steps per second. Return it in kbps. Treat `0 * log 0` as 0.
hints: `math.prod(strides)` gives `M`. Steps per second is `fs / M`.
A codebook with `n_codes` entries costs `log2(n_codes)` bits per step when each code has a fixed length.
`np.log2(p)` is `-inf` where `p = 0`. Select `p[p > 0]` before you take the logarithm.
Compare with a tolerance when you test whether `kbps / per_codebook` is a whole number.
